title: Switch Pirate Ignored Nintendo’s Lawsuit, Now He Owes $4.5 Million
text:
After suing a former Reddit moderator in October 2025 for pirating Switch games , a Washington court has ordered the individual in question to pay Nintendo $4.5 million in damages.
According to a September 25 TorrentFreak report , US District Judge Lauren King ordered former r/SwitchPirates moderator James "Archbox" Williams to cough up $4.5 million in damages to Nintendo after the company accused him of operating several pirate shops to illegally decrypt and distribute Switch games to the public.
The lawsuit, which was filed in a Washington federal court in June 2024, stated that Williams had been running this racket since at least 2019, using "circumvention device" software to bypass the company's systems and gain access to over 30 Nintendo Switch games. This includes titles like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom , Mario Kart 8 Deluxe , and Super Smash Bros. Ultimate .
Williams reportedly ignored the complaint at the time, which prompted Nintendo to seek the statutory maximum of $150,000 per title in October 2025. And just this week, Judge King agreed with Nintendo's request, stating that Williams was aware of the case, as he both hired a lawyer to object to a Google subpoena and continued posting on Reddit but opted to not respond to the company's lawsuit.
In one screenshot saved by TorrentFreak , Williams called himself a "pirate" in a Reddit thread, clarifying that he--and others like him--won't "give Nintendo $50 for a game" when there are "months of releases unavailable anywhere."
It's a bit like that I Think You Should Leave skit , where Tim Robinson, in a hot dog suit, drives a hot-dog-shaped car through a suiting store and is "looking for the guy who did this." Both Judge King and Nintendo know the guy who did it, and they want him to pay a lot for his actions.
"The last factor also weighs heavily in favor of the statutory maximum penalty because NOA's complaint contains well-supported and extensive allegations that Williams knew the videogames were copyrighted but willfully undertook his copying and distribution efforts anyway," Judge King concluded in the suit. "Williams' egregious infringement activities merit substantial punishment here."
In addition to the $4.5 million in damages, Williams has also been ordered to cease all illegal distributions of Switch games through a permanent injunction. This includes barring him from encouraging others to download pirated games or bypass Nintendo's systems to do so, disabling his myriad pirate shops, and deactivating his social media accounts. According to TorrentFreak, much of this has already happened, as Williams' Discord, Instagram, Reddit, Telegram, TikTok, and X accounts are gone. Further, some of the pirate shops Williams ran were taken offline after Nintendo sent a cease-and-desist letter in March 2024.
For Nintendo, this is another win against thieves who think they can get away with pirating the company's games . According to the lawsuit, the company wanted to both stop Williams' infringing activities and use him as an example of what happens when you go up against the ever-litigious Mario maker. Be careful. Those white gloves might serve you papers.

title: Yes, Beyond Good & Evil 2 Is Somehow Still In Development
text:
No news is good news, they say. They also say that some news, however little, is good news, too, and girl, do we have some news: Ubisoft's struggling action-adventure game Beyond Good & Evil 2 is still alive despite remaining in development hell.
Ubisoft Bordeaux's lead writer and associate narrative director Rik Godwin took to Bluesky on September 22 to provide a brief update on the game.
"Odd sort of non-announcement but for the past few months I've been working on Beyond Good & Evil 2 in a support/consultant role," Godwin, who was a writer on Assassin's Creed Shadows , said. "I am allowed to say this, I checked."
It makes sense that Ubisoft Bordeaux would assist with Beyond Good & Evil 2. According to IGN , Ubisoft Montpellier, which is leading the project's development, is just south of the Bordeaux studio. And although Ubisoft Bordeaux was the lead developer on both 2023's Assassin's Creed Mirage and Shadows' 2025 expansion Claws of Awaji , that studio typically operates in a support role for Ubisoft's myriad other teams.
This minor update comes nearly 10 years after Ubisoft re-revealed Beyond Good & Evil 2 at E3 2017, and nearly 20 years after Ubisoft announced the action-adventure sequel all the way back in May 2008. There have been some rumblings of progress, with Ubisoft posting hints that development was ongoing in November 2025 and January 2026 . However, whatever progress that has been made has been slow at best and invisible at worst.
Although there's no release date at the moment, Ubisoft has continued to swear that Beyond Good & Evil 2 will be released in due time. Just don't expect it anytime soon, and at this rate, maybe don't expect it in this current console generation.

title: This Diablo 4 Trick Lets You Become Stronger Than Ever, But It Might Not Be Intended
text:
Diablo 4 players are decking themselves out in full sets of Mythic Unique gear as part of Season 15, resulting in characters that are more powerful than ever before. Whether that was Blizzard's goal, or this is simply a mistake of some kind, is currently up for debate.
It's about as big of a change from one season to the next that Diablo 4 has ever experienced. Back in Season 14, Blizzard added the "crafted" item tag to Mythic Uniques made via the Horadric Cube, Blacksmith, or Jeweler, with a limit of only one crafted Mythic being equippable at a time. Even if you had the Resplendent Sparks resource needed to make more Mythics, you couldn't use them. Instead, you had to rely on good old-fashioned luck to find natural Mythic drops without the crafted tag.
The changes weren't popular , so Blizzard walked it back mid-season , and has made further improvements as part of the latest season, Hell's Legacy. Mythics made by the Blacksmith or Jeweler are no longer considered "crafted," while ones made via the cube still are. Once again, players could have several Mythics of your own creation equipped at once, much like the previous seasons.
However, for players with more sparks than they know what to do with, there is technically a way to get around the "crafted" tag.
It takes combining three of the same Mythic Unique (not exactly an easy task) in the cube using the Recycle Uniques recipe, resulting in a new version of that same item. While the item will have all new stat rolls, the key here is that this recycled Mythic Unique won't have the "crafted" tag, letting players equip as many of them as they can create.
The result is players running around with full sets of Mythic gear, something we've never seen before in Diablo 4. This would be a huge problem and could completely break the game in many ways, if it weren't harder to do than it sounds.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u9IHlOYCrbg
Considering it costs 15 Resplendent Sparks to just create one Mythic Unique this way, it's definitely a huge time investment. To do this trick with all 12 gear slots would cost an enormous 180 Sparks, something that seems nearly impossible for an average player and would require an ungodly amount of grinding and farming. That hasn't stopped some of the game's most dedicated content creators from doing exactly that, however, as highlighted by Wudijo .
Whether the ability to create non-crafted Mythic Uniques this way is an intentional choice on Blizzard's part or an oversight remains to be seen. Diablo 4's next update is slated for September 29, but the 3.2.2 patch notes make no mention of this trick and instead are mostly bug fixes.
Overall, Season 15 seems to have been well-received by players after the largely unpopular Season 14. The season finally added Diablo to Diablo 4, as players relive past Prime Evil encounters from previous Diablo games and rub shoulders with none other than the legendary Deckard Cain.
Diablo 4 won't receive new expansions going forward, but it is set to receive a new class, the Amazon , in the first half of next year. Meanwhile, Blizzard is hard at work on Diablo 5 , set to release in 2029, and has already revealed three of its playable classes .

title: Microsoft CEO Attempts To Kill Remaining Xbox Goodwill
text:
After Xbox laid off 1,600 employees over the summer, Microsoft's gaming division followed up with more layoffs and studio closures this week. In the wake of these events, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is taking a look at the bright side and praising Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's actions as a necessary step.
"There's some amount of streamlining the team is doing, and Asha is doing, which is great to see," said Nadella during his appearance on the Sources Podcast . He also noted that he feels "fantastic about the IP we have right now. If I look at the studios, the IP portfolio we have, and our ability to then take that and produce great games going forward, I feel fantastic."
"We have to invent the right sustainable business model that allows us to deliver gaming to more and more people," added Nadella.
Regarding AI, Nadella questioned why Western consumers are so skeptical about the technology compared to other parts of the world.
"I think we've not given [AI] breathing space," said Nadella. "In fact ... I was reading the Gallup poll on AI and it's not good in the West. What's also very interesting … it's not a uniform thing around the world. And in fact that's the thing we should ask: 'What did we get wrong in the West that these other countries may not have?' Why are people in Nigeria more optimistic about AI than in the United States?' And I think we should reflect on it and my belief here is the industry [has] to earn the trust [and] show the benefits to both consumers and enterprises and the communities. And then ... we'll be fine. But without it, just any amount of just celebrating technology for technologies sake is not working."
Prominent AI skeptic Ed Zitron has blamed Xbox's precarious position on " catastrophic mismanagement " by Microsoft and AI bets that didn't pan out. Even after the most recent layoffs, there are indications that more job cuts are coming to Xbox .

title: 波兰资料片之不完全流程记录
text:
过场
近几年，因为各种各样的原因，我很少出差。直到今年夏天，相对自由了一些，借着点机缘巧合，我接到一位神秘友人（NPC 之 Damian）的邀请，与多位国内同行和朋友一起，开启了一段为期一周的剧情，前往波兰。
写下这篇文章，已经是大约两个月后，不长不短的这段时间过去，一些不那么重要的细节确实已经模糊——人类的记忆就是如此，自带降噪和提炼机制，就像游戏的任务记录。
《展翅翱翔》（Wingspan）是独立游戏发行领域颇具代表性的跨国合作案例：实体桌游系美国桌游设计师 Elizabeth Hargrave 作品，波兰工作室 Monster Couch 取得授权并开发数字版本，数字版 Steam 中国区发行则由 indienova 负责
主线：双城记
谈及波兰的游戏产业分布，至少有五座城市可以一提。
华沙（Warsaw）： 波兰首都，政治、经济、文化中心，CD PROJEKT RED 与 11 bit studios 总部所在地。
克拉科夫（Kraków）： 波兰软件产业聚集地，拥有雅盖隆大学（Jagiellonian University）、AGH 科技大学（AGH University of Krakow）等多所理工科大学，Bloober Team（《寂静岭 2》重制版）与 Fool's Theory（《奇唤士》）等团队所在地，每年举办游戏产业会议 Digital Dragons Conference。
波兹南（Poznań）： 游戏产业大会 Game Industry Conference（GIC）每年在此举办，通常与中东欧地区规模最大的娱乐和多媒体展会 Poznań Game Arena 同期举行。
弗罗茨瓦夫（Wrocław）： 弗罗茨瓦夫理工大学、Techland 总部所在地。
卡托维兹（Katowice）： 波兰电竞产业中心，2025 年之前，世界顶级电竞赛事 Intel Extreme Masters Katowice 每年在此举办。
以上这些城市，也都有着规模不等的独立游戏开发者社区，而我的两个重要剧情触发点，依次在华沙和卡托维兹。
华沙的这场活动名为 MeetUp65: Brama do Chin（MeetUp65: 通往中国之路），由波兰创新产业中心策划。规则为“阵营战”：一方是来自中国的游戏媒体（机核、游研社、触乐、IGN 中国、A9VG、3DM、游民星空、INDIENOVA）和线上内容分发平台（小黑盒、杉果、抖音、B 站、小红书、迅雷游戏），一方是波兰本土的独立游戏工作室/开发者，双方需要在一天的会议时间内，根据各自需求，完成数百场 1 对 1 的交流。
为了实现快速 Meet Up，主办方为这场活动预先设置了匹配机制：活动前两周，与会的波兰工作室/开发者提前拿到即将到访的中方嘉宾名单，并表明是否有与其中任何一位接触的意向。所有意向信息汇总后，我拿到手的，就是一张中方 X 波方的轮转配对排班表，每位参会者的一天都被划分为多个时段，每个时段与对方阵营中的一位 Meet Up。
密集的 Meet UP 排班表，这只是前半部分
具体到我个人，在那一天，大约有 31 场迷你会议，每场 10 分钟，整个过程相当紧凑：基本上是按桌牌坐定后，便有第一组旗鼓相当的对手（波兰工作室/开发者）前来匹配，主要是介绍自己团队的项目。由于衔接近乎无缝，10 分钟的时限也几乎没有弹性，每当进行到差不多 8 分钟，就会有工作人员（NPC 之 Marek）大声提示——虽然我听不懂他喊出的波兰语单词，但根据事先说明过的规则，大家都知道，这意味着本段 10 分钟的交流还剩最后 2 分钟。于是，接下来 120 秒的“加速输出”后，伴随另一声结束指令，所有波兰工作室代表起身离席，快步走向下一个目标桌位，开始新一轮的匹配。
会议开始前，我的桌位
最远端的位置，我对面坐的是 Monster Couch 的创始人 Chris
在如此短的时间里，大家能交流的内容相对有限，通常是双方简要介绍各自的作品或业务，表达可能的合作方向等。其间能听到的最多的句式是：
“不好意思，我是个人开发者，所以没有名片......”
“我们是一个很小的团队......”
“这是我（工作室）的游戏，它是一款......”
“我们的游戏已经积累了一些愿望单，中国区是愿望单的第二大（或者最大）来源......”
“中国是个很大的市场，如何让我们的游戏被更多中国玩家知道......”
......
对于许多话题，我们并没有时间详谈，所以互换名片，添加联系方式是最重要的环节，通常也是一轮交流的收尾。
显然，除了业务对接外，这天还是一个数值验证关卡，对参与者的体力值提出了相当高的要求。而我蹩脚的英语，在这么严格的时限内将将够用，如果再多 5 分钟，话题一发散，估计就撑不住了。
接续白天的活动，当晚还有一场独立游戏圆桌讨论，主要是针对波兰工作室/开发者感兴趣的中国游戏市场相关问题进行分享和解答。一直到提问环节结束，我们返回酒店，已经是当地时间 22：00 以后（此时还没意识到这将是行程常态 T_T），满满一天下来，输入的信息接近溢出，收获则是许多微信、Discord 新会话，还有厚了一些的名片盒。
木制名片卡，这也是我的名片盒厚了的原因
第二个剧情触发点卡托维兹，是 RTS 游戏玩家相对熟悉的地方。2023 年 IEM《星际争霸 2》世界总决赛‌中，我国选手 Oliveira 在卡托维兹的 Spodek 体育馆（飞碟体育馆）战胜韩国选手 Maru 获得冠军，与此一墙之隔，就是卡托维兹国际会议中心——我们抵达的周末，一年一度的游戏产业会议卡托维兹夏季版（GIC Sprint Katowice）在此举办，我猜这也是我们的行程选定在 6 月的主要原因之一。
Spodek 体育馆近景，2025 年 6 月，电子竞技联盟（ESL）宣布 IEM 卡托维兹将迁移至克拉科夫，飞碟体育馆的电竞辉煌将暂时停滞
如果以市区人口规模衡量，传统工业城市卡托维兹大致是波兰的第 10 大城市，常住人口约 30 万。相应的，GIC Sprint Katowice 的规模也精干而不铺张，它和其他大型游戏行业展会有着类似的框架，集合了游戏展陈、行业会议和商务接洽功能。为期两天的展会中，我们同样有两条专属任务线，其一是团体任务，参加面向中国市场的 Go to China Pitch 专场：由当前有开发中的、即将上线的游戏项目的波兰团队，面向中国媒体和平台现场推介。另一条是个人任务线，也就是与大型游戏展会伴生的商务对接衍生场 Meet to Match：参会者可根据需求，与其他行业人士通过 GIC 官方 App 预约短会议，然后在指定的会议室和桌位进行 1 对 1 面谈——和华沙的 MeetUp65 形式完全相同，区别在于这次是没有排班表的完全自由匹配。
这些被锁定的时段之外，便可自行活动。与国际性的大展会相比，GIC Sprint Katowice 的人流密度要小一些，所以只要你有兴趣，几乎可以在一个周末体验完全场的所有游戏。有意思的是，我还在现场遇到了几位既不出展，也未在分论坛发言，更不单纯是游客的独立开发者，闲聊几句才知道，原来他们当前并没有在某个项目中任职，而这次展会，刚好是找工作的契机之一。
在我能接触到的范围里，论及政府对游戏产业的重视和支持，波兰或许可以排在最前列。大约在 2016 年，波兰国家研究与发展中心（NCBR）就正式推出游戏产业专项计划 GameINN，扶持行业技术发展，并明确游戏产业为未来波兰经济发展的重要方向之一；2018 年起，波兰开始以国家展区（展台）形式参与世界大型游戏展会（现在也包括上海 WePlay）；2023 年，波兰文化部门推出电子游戏支持计划 Program Wsparcia Gier Wideo，鼓励本土的中小游戏开发团队从文化创意层面出发，推出更多优秀作品；2025 年底，“波兰游戏产业圆桌会议”在 GIC 期间举行，与游戏产业紧密联系的政府机构代表围绕融资、立法、国内外推广以及专业化 4 个领域探讨了游戏开发提案，并于 2026 年初正式发布圆桌会议报告，其中明确表示：这些意见将成为制定波兰游戏产业发展战略的基础。接下来，在今年十月，首届波兰电子游戏日即将亮相，计划以 GOG 平台的线上活动为核心，同期举办多场线上和线下配套活动，波兰也将成为全球首个在国家层面设立此类官方主题活动日的国家。
支线：步行模拟
华沙
按时间线顺序，我们作为考察团抵达波兰的第一项正式活动，是参加波兰文化与国家遗产部的座谈会（MeetUp65 的前一天）。在这个半日谈和此后几天的日程空隙，导览 NPC（NPC 之 Damian）生怕我们体力回满白白溢出，贴心地为我们排满了城市观光。
我们在波兰的“足迹地图”：华沙—维利奇卡—卡托维兹—克拉科夫
波兰总统府，斜对面就是波兰文化与国家遗产部
华沙老城区，圣十字教堂，肖邦的心脏安放在这里；我们停留过的波兰城市，街道都同样干净，不时可见各种墙绘，绝大部分街区也相当安全
华沙的街景，可以归纳为新，一部分是现代发展的新，一部分是重建历史的新。作为首都，华沙新城区和我们日常所见的现代化城市面貌大抵相似。而老城区就有些意思了：二战期间，华沙城超过 85%的面积被毁，1945 年至 1951 年重建时，重建办公室并未把目标设定在将市容恢复至战前模样，而是尽可能依托未受损的历史建筑、街道、城墙等，参考档案文献，力求重现 18 世纪晚期波兰的历史风貌。可以说，从历史文化角度审视，华沙老城是也不是原来那座，若从观光游览角度，华沙老城正处于新中有老、老而未旧的限定赏味期。
维拉诺宫：位于华沙维拉努夫区，在两次世界大战中都幸免于难，是波兰最重要的古迹和艺术博物馆之一
卡托维兹
接下来让我们先跳过维利奇卡，快进到工业城市卡托维兹。在此参展（GIC）的两天里，我们的探图路线相对集中，基本在酒店至展馆沿线活动。不过，由于 GIC 是当地时间每天上午 10：00 开场，主办方特意在展会首日给我们插入了晨间 1 小时徒步——Nikoszowiec 街区（景区）速览。
Nikoszowiec 全景，街区很精致，适合散步慢游，有旅游攻略将 Nikoszowiec 称为红砖秘境 /图片：网络
历史上，这个街区原本是当地煤矿工人的住宅区，形制类似矩形围屋，每个网格单元的四条边是住宅，中央则是公共生活区域。现在，Nikoszowiec 已发展成为文创景区，传统的红砖建筑、红漆窗框、斜倾窗台延续下来，成为整个街区的统一视觉要素。窗台向下倾斜不难理解，这里位于煤矿产区周边，可以减少积尘；至于最初采用红色涂装，理由也很充分，红漆既廉价又在矿场大量使用，是当时最容易获得的涂料。
工业历史留下的装饰风格
克拉科夫
一周访问结束之际，飞往不同城市的考察团成员分批次从克拉科夫国际机场出发，这也是本次行程的最后一站。克拉科夫距卡托维兹只有不到 1 小时车程，作为最晚登机（当地时间晚上）的北京 5 人组，我们决定一早出门，也就多了半日游的时间。
回家之前，象征性采购是应有之意。快速打卡曾为波兰王室住所的瓦维尔城堡后，我们沿着克拉科夫老城区购物街，辗转了几家琥珀店，最后在一间名为“Game Over”的游戏商店连逛带歇，顺便蹭蹭空调，也算达成了一个应景的收尾。
波罗的海琥珀，波兰的代表性特产之一；北部沿海城市格但斯克是波罗的海琥珀重要的产地和加工中心，而波兰最大的旅游城市之一克拉科夫，差不多就是格但斯克之外最适合入手琥珀的地方；图为克拉科夫旅游购物街纺织会馆的琥珀饰品与琥珀镶嵌国际象棋
Game Over，旅程也即将结束
说来又很巧，我们在的这几天，正好赶上波兰天气的大版本更新。行前攻略显示，波兰已经连续阴雨半个月，考虑到主办方应该不会让我们淋着，我最终在背包整理环节释放了原本留给雨伞的空间。但实际上，我们的 City Walk 伴随着天天放晴，持续高温，以及当地政府发布的 XX 年一遇的高温预警。从事实来看，概率学和我的运气，至少有一个的数值存在问题。
支线：地下城探索
虽然都可归为步行游览，但在我这里，维利奇卡盐矿必须单独成为一条支线，因为一个字，大。
这座盐矿是波兰的国宝级景观，最浅处在地下 64 米，最深处约 327 米，从 13 世纪开始持续开采，一直到 20 世纪末停产，并于同期被认定为波兰国家古迹，列入联合国教科文组织濒危世界遗产名录，现在以旅游景区、博物馆和疗养中心的综合体形式对外开放。700 年的盐业开采，为这个地下世界留下了约 2350 个矿室，以及连通这些矿室的超过 250 公里长的矿道。
当你穿行在分层的矿道中，回旋而下或蜿蜒前行，真有些箱庭世界的味道。四顾所见一切的基础都是盐：盐雕、采盐设备、盐矿工人的工作生活痕迹等。大部分矿道的四壁其实就是裸露的盐矿，可随时品鉴的那种。
建议优先品尝不太容易尝到的地方，这不是调高难度，那些比较舒服就能舔食的位置，应该已经有许多游客尝过
沿着单向观光路线，我们途经的许多矿室都不大，纵深不过几米，多是采盐工具或盐雕展示。
雕塑主题主要有三类：神话（历史）传说、盐矿生产场景、宗教相关
另有些空间就远超预期了，比如，当你从上层走下，初见圣金加礼拜堂（St. Kinga's Chapel）前，会很难想象地下 100 米处能有这样的硕大空间：惊人的挑高、宽展如小型广场的厅堂、巨型水晶吊灯——被几乎布满了宗教题材（场景或人物）浮雕的四壁围拢。
圣金加礼拜堂：长期在光照受限的地下环境工作，矿工们在日常工作开始前进行祷告，在重要宗教节日参加弥撒，是非常必然的需求
根据历史记载，圣金加礼拜堂是在开采完一整块巨大的岩盐矿体后形成的矿室。其入口附近，可以看到三位重要雕刻家的纪念牌：约瑟夫·马尔科夫斯基（Józef Markowski）、托马什·马尔科夫斯基（Tomasz Markowski）和安东尼·维罗德克（Antoni Wyrodek）。他们有着相似的成长轨迹，都是从一线矿工逐步自学跻身为雕刻家，并从 19 世纪末开始，接力完成了礼拜堂的许多雕刻工作。有意思的是，纪念铭牌区目前尚留有一个空位，或许未来有一天，会有新一代雕刻家在此留下姓名。
到如今，维利奇卡盐矿内部还有华沙厅（Warszawa Chamber，约 680 平方米）、Jan Haluszka Chamber 等营业场所，可承接宴席、会务等活动，甚至还有地下住宿项目 Słowacki Chamber 和矿工酒馆（Karczma Górnicza）。尽管许多人（包括我）可能对地下光照环境不太习惯，但若是依照法环遗风，盐矿入口完全可以留有数行手书：前有绝景。
据导游介绍，维利奇卡盐矿支线还有另一种打开方式。我们此行走过的是游客路线，附带一条游览时长约 1.5 小时的博物馆分支环路。在此之外，还有一条传说中的矿工路线，需要游客穿戴全套下矿装备进行体验。是的，当下的维利奇卡盐矿仍然有矿工下井工作，不过工作内容不再是采盐，而是对整个矿区例行维护，毕竟对于这类人工开凿的地下空间而言，时间带来的基建老化是很大的风险。
纪念品店必不可少：盐灯、盐雕、纯盐冰箱贴，还有不在图中的盐味巧克力
彩蛋
既见波兰，怎么能少的了 CDPR、GOG、11 bit studios.......只是交互内容着实不在预料之内，权算作彩蛋吧 O(∩_∩)O。所有彩蛋行程都发生在一天之内，MeetUp65 的后一天，也是我们在华沙的最后一天。
CDPR
相当不巧，CDPR 正在全力开发《巫师 4》，且当前各游戏项目并不在宣发节点，所以尽管提前签署了保密协议，但我们只是参观了 CDPR 的非工作区域，未能获得更多消息。正如同行的伙伴所说，这份保密协议就是最需要保密的部分了。
CDPR 前台旁边的角色墙
CDPR 园区，由旧仓库改造而成的内部酒吧
GOG
去年年底，GOG 已从资本层面和 CDPR 剥离，不过其办公地址并未变动，仍在 CDPR 园区。目前，GOG 正通过 Dreamlist 机制（平台用户共同投票产生愿望单，作为 GOG 团队选择下一款引入平台的游戏时的参考）将更多早期游戏复活并留存下来，一些（中国）国产经典游戏已在计划中——其中包含多个国内玩家耳熟能详的 IP，部分已经取得授权，处于兼容性优化或移植阶段。
GOG 办公室陈列区，架上有我曾经无力购买的正版《无冬之夜 2》（Neverwinter Nights 2）
在游戏保存方面，实体收藏、源代码保存等可以让游戏作品保留最初面世的样子。GOG 目前所做的游戏保护，则着力于让经典游戏在当前的软硬件环境下以相对贴近时代的面貌运行，并力图提供永久维护。两相结合，再加上对游戏设计文档、开发者访谈、说明书、包装、广告、版本记录、社群衍生内容等资料的系统性发掘和整理，游戏作为媒介或可具备长期被体验和研究的基础。
11 bit studios
参观 CDPR 的同一天下午，我们访问了 11 bit studios。当时正值《多重人生》的 DLC“最终变量”发售前夕，以及《冰汽时代 2》的 DLC“灰烬誓约”上线，两款游戏的制作人专门在现场进行了创作分享。接下来的几个小时乍听起来可能不太科学，我们在 11 bit studios 的荣誉陈列室体验了包饺子，就是字面意义上的手工包饺子。
作为土生土长的中国北方人，我第一次了解到饺子（Pierogi，波兰语，特指波兰饺子，当前写法已经是复数形式）也是波兰的传统美食之一，迄今已有数百年历史。至于其起源则有多种解释，东方传入说与本土演化说各有流传，并未有决定性的史料。
11 bit stuidos 荣誉墙
荣誉墙对侧，万事俱备，准备开包；图中的女性厨师介绍说，她曾在上海开过多年波兰饺子店，但我也不在国内吃波兰饺子，这不就卡流程了吗
波兰饺子和中式饺子的区别主要在于馅料。其中咸口的和中式饺子比较接近，基本是肉+菜或纯素馅，有些会有奶酪调味，比如土豆泥奶酪饺子。甜口的馅料基本是水果加白糖，属于当地特色，也要看食客习惯与否。实际包饺子的时候，会发现包水果饺子的难度明显更高，因为果馅加糖后会出水，一旦沾到饺子皮的边缘，就很容易粘不住。
最终，我们这群水平参差的杂牌军分为几组，还是各自现包现煮出 2 盘波兰饺子，一是经典土豆泥奶酪馅，一是草莓馅。 必须 抛开卖相不提，吃起来都挺不错，这当然是因为 大家上得展会下得厨房 两位带教厨师带领大家按标准配比调制好了馅料。最后一批水饺出锅后，两位大厨非常热心地帮助我们快速完成了打包，我猜可能是被抛开的卖相会有损些什么吧......
Pinball Station
Pinball Station 是此行最令我惊喜的地方。它并不在最初的行程单上，是在我们抵达华沙后才被告知存在的神秘环节。这是一座收藏有超过 160 台实体弹珠台游戏机和古早街机柜的私人博物馆，也是一处游戏开发者、爱好者的夜间娱乐场所。
稍晚我们会有一篇文章专门介绍 Pinball Station，现在就到这里为止。
Pinball Station，上下两层，位于华沙市中心新老城区交界线旁靠老城区一侧的旧厂房中
NPC
我所接触到的波兰友人都很友好，以下几位尤其务实，一定程度上可作为波兰独立游戏领域的联络人，在这篇文章里，就暂时委屈他们以 NPC 的身份露面。
（除了 Damian，我和其他三位都是初次认识，只有短暂几天接触，以下仅作简要的不全面介绍。如有切实需求，你可以通过 LinkedIn 找到他们）
Damian
我和 Damian Jaskowski  认识，应该是在 2020 年的上海 WePlay 文化展，当时他发送给我的名片上印着一个邓姓中文名字，下面写着“波兰大使馆文化处 游戏专员”。这是我第一次在名片上看到类似头衔，也是我对波兰政府“重视游戏产业”的印象的来源。
目前，Damian 已从大使馆文化处卸任，仍以中国游戏市场专家身份和波兰政府部门紧密合作，同时担任波兰独立游戏基金会（Fundacja Indie Games Polska，IGP）的中国市场协调人和 11 bit studios 的中国市场营销负责人。
Damian 为促进中国与波兰的游戏产业交流做了很多工作，包括但不限于组织协调双方行业代表互访、参展（如本次考察团），并撰有由波兰驻华大使馆文化处与波兰独立游戏基金会联合发布的《中国游戏市场报告》（CHIŃSKI RYNEK GIER，2018）。由于行业和市场环境变化，这份报告在 2023 至 2024 年由 Damian 完成了更新和扩展，也就是曾被国内游戏媒体广泛报道过的 《面向中国游戏市场的开发者指南》 （Game Developer’s Guide to the Chinese Market）。
现在，中文环境下，周围的人都称呼他“大面”，即 Damian 的谐音
Marek
Marek Czerniak 也身兼数职，当前以联合创始人身份出任波兰独立游戏基金会董事会主席，同时担任非营利组织波兰国家电子和电信商会（KIGEiT）旗下游戏开发分会（Gamedev Poland）的副主席，也作为游戏行业代表入选波兰行业能力委员会游戏与游戏开发领域（Sektorowa Rada ds. Kompetencji – Gaming i GameDev）成员。
官方身份之外，他作为开发者联合创办了独立游戏工作室 Atomic Wolf，担任首席执行官兼创意总监，工作室旗下作品包括动作冒险游戏 《解放者》 （Liberated）、 《非套路奇幻游戏》 （Yet Another Fantasy Title）等。
Kuba
Jakub Wójcik （Kuba）同样是波兰独立游戏界的老资历，曾担任 Star Drifters 工作室的业务负责人，并创办了波兰首个专注于独立游戏的行业服务和媒体平台 1ndie World。现为游戏营销机构 better. gaming agency 的联合创始人，同时以联合创始人身份兼任波兰独立游戏基金会执行主席，全面负责机构的日常运营。
小插曲：去波兰前，因护照过期需要换发，波兰独立游戏基金会为我出具了邀请函，签名处正是 Kuba 的名字。后续在华沙的 MeetUp 活动中，我先和 Kuba 的同事 Maciej 见了面。几个小时后，Maciej 发送给我一条 Discord 消息，“现在 Kuba 在会场，你可以抓到他，他穿着《黑神话：悟空》的圆领衫，戴着 better. gaming 的帽子。”但正如之前提及，那天的日程过于紧凑，我完全没时间巡场，不过很快，在某个间隙，一位身材魁梧的红帽老哥坐在了我的对面，他身上的黑色 T 恤印着《黑神话》的 Logo。随后几天里，我们又多次碰面，还一起在 Pinball Station 进行了一场弹珠台对战.......
在 GIC 现场的合照，左起为 Kuba、我、Marek，发布照片已征得出镜人同意
Hanna
Hanna Marszałkowska 是波兰游戏行业的重要组织者角色，长期参与维特鲁威基金会（Vitruvio Foundation，波兰非营利组织，GIC 主办方，旨在推动波兰及中东欧地区的游戏开发行业发展）、波兰独立游戏基金会等机构的工作，尤其在 GIC 担任重要职能，其官网将 Hanna 列为赞助商对接负责人、活动安全及行为规范投诉负责人。
而在 GIC 的姊妹活动 GIC Sprint Katowice，Hanna 就是六边形战士，她熟悉所有游戏的展位，有所有人的联系方式，每一位和我聊过的开发者（参会者）都告诉我有问题找 Hanna，我也确实找了——当我想联系其中一位确定出席但不知道在哪里的开发者时，坐镇咨询台的 Hanna 直接掏出手机拨打了这位开发者的电话，并告诉我“半个小时后回来这里，那位开发者也会到。”说实话，我很久没有见到这种工作场合无预告直接打电话的情景了，但很好，很有用，很高效。
Hanna 的丈夫也是波兰独立游戏领域的代表性人物，不过我此行未能见到
再会
回国后，我每隔几天都会收到一两封来自波兰朋友的邮件，也会时不时在 Discord 看到波兰工作室最新的游戏项目介绍。按照规律，如果没有某些合作契机，这种联系会随时间越来越弱。不过很快，也就是两个月后，波兰工作室将组团参加今年的上海 WePlay，大家又要再见面了。这样看来，不论在哪里，展会（展馆）都完全可以算是行业交流、跨国友谊的强化建筑吧。
最后，感谢波兰大使馆文化处、波兰创新产业中心、波兰独立游戏基金会的邀请，一去七日，此行不虚。

title: A pro CS2 player told me he ditched his Superstrike gaming mouse for the older Superlight 2 because it was 'inconsistent'
text:
I found yxngstxr's candidness fantastic, here, considering we were at a Logitech G Play event when he said these words to me—an event surrounding the launch of the X3 Superstrike, no less. I trusted what he was saying: he liked the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike and tried it for a while, but found it inconsistent, and had heard about it having a front-weighted balance.
The front balance is something I'd noticed, and it seems Logitech has, too, because the new X3 Superstrike has its weighting more centrally balanced—one of the biggest upgrades to the new one. It will be interesting to see whether yxngstxr switches to the X3 now.
Another CS2 pro, Oscar 'Azuwu' Bell, reminded me: "M0nesy [one of the best CS2 players], before the major, he was on the Superstrike, and for the major he went back to the Superlight."
For my part, I tend to think that shape is king and whatever fits your hand and your grip most comfortably is what will serve you better. Which is in part why I'm hoping that Logitech releases more mouse shapes with the Superstrike's HITS system in there. I did ask Logi about this—perhaps a 'Dex' shape—but the company wouldn't say yes. Perhaps notably, I didn't get a 'no', either.

title: 'Everything is hard. But it turns out that’s not society’s problem, that’s my problem,' says Jensen Huang about AI development
text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has appeared on The Ezra Klein Show to discuss AI development, amid a wider discussion around its responsible usage and safety. Klein spoke to the Nvidia chief about multiple topics, including the AI industry's potential effects on the job market. "I tend to be a bit of a skeptic on mass job loss, but I want to air the case for it out here with you well," says Klein.
Klein then asks a question about lessons that could be learned from the past, regarding protecting US jobs from Mexico and China, and the acceleration of AI's ability to be slotted into new roles: "So the lessons of the past that you’re taking some comfort in, they should actually make you more, not less, worried about the future."
"I’m always worried about the future," Huang responds. "That’s why I work so hard. I’m a, if you will, responsible optimist.
"I have great responsibilities. I take my work extremely seriously. There are a lot of things that can go wrong. We’re pushing across every layer of the technology stack. Everything is hard," Huang continues.
"But it turns out that’s not society’s problem, that’s my problem. For society, what they should know is this: We’re going to build our company, we’re going to build our technology, I’m going to do my work so incredibly seriously that what they get to enjoy is my optimism. I do the same with my children. I do the same with my family."
(Image credit: Nvidia) Certainly, the current AI debate seems to be dominated by an unease surrounding the potential negative impacts of the rapid advancement of the tech, from job losses to cybersecurity concerns . However, Huang seems to think that the upsides of this speedy development process might put some people's minds at ease.
"What we want to do, I believe," said Huang, "is to channel all of our worries into helping people be inspired by this technology and use it. Use it so that the technology doesn’t just impact them, that it benefits them."
After Klein posited the statistic that 79% of American think AI will reduce the number of jobs , and that AI advancement means the tech is more capable of replacing people at speed, Huang responds:
"That coin has exactly two sides. Because the technology is so capable and because it’s so smart, it is also easier to use. You are empowered by that technology more easily than any technology in human history."
The Nvidia CEO then goes on to give an example of how computers use specialised coding languages, but now, thanks to AI, "You just have to speak human."
(Image credit: JOSH EDELSON / AFP via Getty Images) "So my point is, on the one hand, yes, there’s the fear of this incredible technology change and how quickly it’s happening. But that quickly is translated in two ways," says Huang.
"When I hear that the technology’s happening quickly, and therefore it should give me anxiety — that’s one way to receive it. The other way to receive it is that it’s advancing so quickly, it’s easier to use. So I should, as quickly as possible, use the technology so that I benefit from this transition, so you benefit from this new industry, and not just be impacted by it."
The inference here feels similar to an idea Huang has expressed previously: those who fail to get on the AI train may end up being left behind . I think the key point, however, is the lack of agency and control individuals feel towards this technological revolution, something that is unlikely to be assuaged by more useful tech—or Huang's optimism, for that matter.
While the Nvidia CEO famously possesses a massive work ethic , and responsible AI usage is a concern he seems to take seriously, I'm not particularly comfortable with the idea that our future seems destined to be shaped by AI tech leaders, and that we should rest easy within their hands.
While Huang may well believe that he has society's best interests in mind, the messaging here hasn't exactly put my own concerns to rest. Stop worrying and learn to love the machine? Something like that, anyway.

title: I made the hot dog vendors in GTA 5 work because Rockstar never did
text:
Los Santos Customs
I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier .
I have filled a yawning void in the soul of Los Santos. I have returned the heart to a heartless world. I am a teacher, a healer, a gardener of human happiness. My efforts have ensured the general flourishing of society and the wellbeing of the spaceship Earth.
Grand Theft Auto 5 has Working Hotdog Vendors now.
Based on the evidence, Rockstar probably intended the hot-dog-purchasing experience in GTA 5 to work much as it did in GTA 4. Why didn't it? A mystery. Dundee was busy working on horse testicles, or whatever it is they do up there, and forgot.
Anyway, it works now. You can now stroll up to the meat-slingers of Los Santos beach and give them five (thanks Obama) dollars for some sort of fleshy tube in a bun. This is electrifying.
The hot dogs heal you, just like in real life, but my favourite part is how they interact with the random-teleport mod I hucked onto my teetering GTA 5 pile just yesterday. One moment you'll be handing over your money, the next you will be perched atop the not-Hollywood sign, lazily chowing down on your grub. Also, the bodyguards that the celebrity mod has assigned you will keep manifesting in thin air next to you before plunging to their deaths. This does not interrupt the hot dog consumption process.
Whatever. (Image credit: Rockstar) It's great. GTA 5 should have been like this the whole time. I can only hope that GTA 6, with its budget of 'roughly Saddam Hussein's gold bullion reserves,' will let you fully experience hot dogs.

title: For Warhorse's 15th birthday, we chatted with its co-founder about the demand for 'grown-up' RPGs, AI, why games are too cheap, and his role in the collapse of communism
text:
Martin Klíma is an iconoclast. As the co-founder of Warhorse Studios, he's responsible for one of the crunchiest, most peculiar, and best RPGs of the last decade—Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, a game few other studios would make. As a former student rabblerouser in the old eastern bloc, he's the only person I've ever spoken to for this job who can say they helped overthrow a government.
He's celebrating the Warhorse's 15th anniversary, a milestone moment in a life that has a lot of them already. "I'd swear it was just yesterday," he says, that he and his fellow co-founder—the eternally fractious Daniel Vávra—were two disaffected devs striking out on their own. But Klíma's career did not begin with the incorporation of Warhorse Studios. It began in the actually existing socialism of Czechoslovakia, in the 1980s.
History check
"I was learning English at school, but it was sort of difficult," recalls Klíma. English educational materials had to be imported from friendly countries, and the only friendly English-speaking country at the time was Ghana, whose materials were miles away from the things Klíma was actually interested in. "I mean no disrespect to the people of Ghana, but it's a bit of an unusual approach to teaching kids English, and so our vocabulary was more about combine harvesters and blast furnaces than swords and dwarves."
What Klíma wanted to read, more than anything, was The Lord of the Rings. But although The Hobbit had been officially published in Czechoslovakia, there was no such luck for LOTR. Around 1987, Klíma was able to get his hands on a copy that someone had brought back from a trip westwards, "but I didn't know enough English to read it, so I had to improve my English. One thing leads to another, and the very fact that we can talk to each other right now is because of JRR Tolkien."
The first movie adaptation of The Hobbit was, in fact, this 1967 animation produced in Prague.
Not long after, Klíma was lucky enough to obtain another imported fantasy treasure: a Dungeons & Dragons Basic Set. "I think for everybody who experiences a role-playing game for the first time, it's an amazing experience: this idea that you can pretend to be somebody else, and you can assume a role and you can live through these amazing adventures in your fantasy."
The game gave him a kind of missionary fervour, a desire to spread the good word of D&D. "I started translating it with my then-girlfriend, now wife, and we went through maybe 80% of the text." The thinking was to publish a translation of the game via Czechoslovakia's underground printing presses; "to officially translate it, officially license it… that was completely unthinkable." Klíma already had experience in this sort of thing—he ran a fanzine that quietly printed popular sci-fi by "[pretending] that they were contributions to our student magazine."
Klíma's dreams of clandestine TTRPG distribution were disrupted by the other part of his life. The group he played D&D with was, in fact, a subset of an independent student union that he and his allies were organising, Stuha . As a student at the University of Prague, Klíma had organised a petition against the demolition of campus buildings. Not, ordinarily, a revolutionary act, but to the flighty Czechoslovakian government it was a "borderline rebellion."
Gorbachev visits Prague, 1987 (in the top right is Czechoslovakian then-president Gustáv Husák). (Image credit: THIERRY ORBAN/Sygma via Getty Images) In decades past, people might have shied away from signing a petition like Klíma's, but things had shifted by the late '80s. "Gorbachev was in power [in the Soviet Union]. There was this talk about 'change' and 'opening' and so on, so people did sign my little petition. In the end, almost 1,000 people signed it, and this really helped me to reach other people who were interested in changing things." It was not Klíma alone—Stuha had other organisers, other borderline and not-so-borderline rebels out to overturn the system—but his was an important role.
Important enough, in fact, that he was chosen to speak for Stuha at a public demonstration on November 17, 1989—International Students' Day, an observance tied to Czech student resistance to Nazi occupation and its subsequent violent repression. Klíma summarises it like so: "There was a big demonstration against the German occupiers in 1939, and on November 17, all the Czech universities were closed [in retaliation] by the Nazi government.
Kneeling students face riot police in Prague, November 1989. (Image credit: LUBOMIR KOTEK/AFP via Getty Images) "It seemed like, if you make a student demonstration on the 50th anniversary of these events, then you must be very safe, because no regime would be so stupid as to fight students, exposing itself to this very obvious comparison to Nazi Germany."
Martin Klíma
"It seemed like, if you make a student demonstration on the 50th anniversary of these events, then you must be very safe, because no regime would be so stupid as to fight students, exposing itself to this very obvious comparison to Nazi Germany."
The Czechoslovakian government, it seemed, did not see things that way. "There was this confrontation with the police, and people were badly beaten… that really radicalized the students and radicalized the rest of the country. In a week, there was a general strike, and by the end of December, Václav Havel was president of Czechoslovakia." The Velvet Revolution—Czechoslovakia's chapter in the Soviet bloc's collapse—had taken place.
Rolling dice
As capitalism took root in Czechoslovakia (and, after 1992 , the Czech Republic), Klíma's sci-fi and gaming ambitions started to look less like a hobby and more like a career. Though he and his partner had been forced to set aside their translation of D&D by the Velvet Revolution, he returned to it in the aftermath. "I wrote a letter to [D&D publisher] TSR, and they never answered me… I even persuaded my relatives in the US to send them letters and faxes… but we never got any response from them. Maybe they thought it was a crazy idea. 'Why would some communist kids want to play D&D?' Maybe it felt absurd to them."
Eventually, inspired by the German TTRPG Das Schwarze Auge , and convinced no one at TSR was going to pick up the phone, Klíma decided to adapt the work he and his partner had already done into something new. "We rewrote most of the text. We created our own classes and our own races. We created our own combat system." That last bit in part because Czechoslovakia did not really possess the means to manufacture 20-sided dice in the early '90s, "so we only had a six-sided die and a 10-sided die."
Slovakians celebrate their independence on New Year's Day 1993, following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia. (Image credit: David Brauchli/Sygma via Getty Images) The result was Dračí doupě . "It became hugely successful, because it was the first fantasy RPG [in Czechoslovakia], and it was really like when it rains in a desert and green sprouts appear… and then I've worked in the games industry ever since." It wasn't long before he moved into computer games with titles like Fish Fillets, Original War, and UFO: Aftermath, developed under the Altar Interactive brand, itself spun off from Altar Publishing, whose name was on Dračí doupě.
Klíma's experience in the games industry between the 1989 revolution and Warhorse's 2011 founding could probably fill books by itself, but a recurring theme in what he told me about those days is frustration with publishers. This came to a head in the late 2000s with an RPG called Vision, led by Czech board and videogame designer Vlaada Chvátil. "This is going to be our big break," Klíma remembers thinking at the time, "This game is going to make history."
Vision in action. (Image credit: Altar Interactive) The game's publisher, CDV Software, was not quite as bullish. "CDV asked us to do some changes, and when we did these changes, they told us that the managing director who signed the original contract with us had left, and now they were no longer interested because of these changes that we made. And then six months later, they went bankrupt as well.
"We were sort of despondent and turned over the company to Bohemia Interactive," says Klíma, with the transfer happening in September 2010. After working on games like Arma for a while, followed by a stint at Codemasters, he was approached by Operation Flashpoint lead designer Viktor Bocan (now one of Warhorse's two creative directors, alongside Prokop Jirsa).
"We were sort of despondent and turned over the company to Bohemia Interactive"
Martin Klíma
Bocan knew a guy with a vision: an achingly realistic RPG set in 15th-century Bohemia, he just needed someone "who is good with Excel, who will do this boring stuff about numbers and plans and so on." The game, of course, was Kingdom Come: Deliverance, and the guy with a vision was Daniel Vávra, its director. Bocan told Vávra to wait right there while he got Klíma on the phone. Warhorse Studios was born.
Thy will be done
One of my first questions to Klíma was, if he could travel back in time and tell his past self how KCD had panned out, would he have been surprised? His answer: the game's success wouldn't have shocked him a jot, but the fact that it actually got made and released would have amazed him.
"We were asking for quite a lot of money," Klíma recalls, and publishers, perhaps predictably, weren't champing at the bit to take a big risk on a studio making a historical RPG that had strong opinions about the order in which you equipped your armour. "It was really difficult at the time… It took us two years to find an investor."
(Image credit: Warhorse Studios) The investor was Czech-American billionaire venture capitalist Zdeněk Bakala. Bakala's cheque gave Klíma and co the means to properly start Warhorse and begin work on KCD, but not enough to complete the game from beginning to end. "We had a really nice demo of the game. We hired an agency. We traveled the world. We talked to, I don't know, 50 different publishers on three continents. Nobody was interested."
The answer: Kickstarter, where it turned out that 35,384 backers were more willing to take a punt on Warhorse's weird medieval RPG than major publishers were. "I think [it's] the idea of a grown-up RPG," Klíma reflected. "I still am bored and tired of all the RPGs where you are this chosen one… Nobody is making a game that would say, 'Okay, this is a big RPG, and you are nobody, and you are not going to become a world saviour. This is a game about an ordinary random person that's doing ordinary, random-person stuff, and at the end, he is just moderately less of a nobody.'"
KCD scratched that itch for over 35,000 people, where "publishers, bless their hearts, are very conservative by the nature of their business… If you have this huge studio, like these established publishers do, it means that your next game is going to cost $100 million… and then you need to sell 4 or 5 million units just to break even, and that's difficult with a new IP.
"I've been in this business for 30 years now, and I only managed to sell one game to a publisher, and that was Original War back in 1997. This experience, trying to sell Kingdom Come to publishers, was really eye-opening in realizing how difficult, almost impossible it is. So it was a great relief and vindication when we saw that the players agreed with us."
All we have to decide is what to do
The first KCD did not light the world on fire—and in Klíma's estimation, is more like Kingdom Come "zero point eight" than a full realisation of the studio's ambitions (that would be KCD2)—but it hit hard enough to let Warhorse expand and to put it on the path to KCD2. "There are of course people who think that KCD1 was a better game than KCD2 and KCD2 is just a watered-down, mainstream, plays-by-itself game for the masses.
"I don't agree… but I can see why somebody thinks that. But still, I think the fact that [KCD1] crashes every three hours is not a good experience," he jokes, "even if you are the most hardcore player ever."
(Image credit: Warhorse Studios) But lots of people, us included, really did like KCD2, and the game was successful enough to send Klíma full circle, from teaching himself English via LOTR books to negotiating the development of a Warhorse-driven LOTR game . "It's clear that because of the success of Kingdom Come, somebody would be willing to entrust us with this license."
Warhorse is now a two-game studio, its teams divided between its LOTR game and an upcoming Kingdom Come adventure. "Now you have people sitting in the same office that used to work together, were part of the same team even recently. And now we have to split them into two groups and focus them each on their own project, and that's quite a challenge."
"It's clear that because of the success of Kingdom Come, somebody would be willing to entrust us with [the LOTR] license."
Martin Klíma
But overall, probably one of those problems it's nice to have. So there's a little paradox: with Warhorse and its ambitions both growing, the wider games industry seems bleaker than it's been in decades, riven with layoffs and ignominious cancellations. For Klíma, it indicates one thing: the growth of videogames as a market has run into limits it can't transcend, even as the progress of technology continues to demand splashier games with bigger goals and larger teams. "You throw more people on the job, and that makes the games more expensive… If the game is more expensive, it needs to sell more units in order for this to be a viable business.
Warhorse is now at a work on a new Kingdom Come adventure and an LOTR game. (Image credit: Warhorse (left) / Wizards of the Coast (right)) "How can you do it? The easiest [way] is you grow the market… But we reached the limit here long ago… If somebody is not playing the games, it's because they don't want to play the games, or they can't afford to play the games. So there's no way unless we teach dogs how to play games." Another way to squeeze more profit? Cut out the middlemen, but the industry's done that too: "We destroyed retail, and we took all their money," jokes Klíma.
"The last thing you can do is to increase the unit price. That would help a lot, but everybody's scared to death about it. Now, hopefully, GTA will blaze the trail…but I think we've run out of options." Meanwhile, technology keeps getting better (though it's maybe been arrested, a little, by the RAMpocalypse) and expectations keep getting higher, in Klíma's assessment.
Klíma wonders if GTA 6 might blaze a trail on higher game prices. (Image credit: Rockstar Games) "I don't see a way out of it other than moving the production to the countries that are cheaper… it's maybe Central and Eastern Europe, maybe China, maybe India, maybe East Asia in general." Good news, perhaps, for Czechia-based Warhorse, but a grim prognosis for North American and west-European development. "I take no pleasure in being a prophet of doom and desolation, but specifically in North America, I think it's a really, really huge problem right now."
The solution much of the executive class is keen on is, of course, AI. For Klíma, many of them have a "simplified mental model" of how it can be introduced that doesn't quite work in reality. Paraphrasing him, that model goes like this: if AI is a 5x force multiplier, he says, many people imagine you can cut a 200-person dev team down to 40. Even if each developer needs their own AI, and each AI costs the same as one dev, you can now do the work of a 200-person dev team while only paying for the cost of an 80-person team.
(Image credit: Deep Silver) Even leaving aside questions of the quality of the AI's output, Klíma doesn't think it works like that. If you have 200 devs and a magical AI multiplies their output by five, players are just going to want the game that 1000-person-dev-team equivalent can make. "This is not a 'get out of jail free' card, the AI. It will not reduce the cost of the game, but it will allow us to create bigger games for the same cost."
I'm more than a little sceptical, as you might expect, but it's clearly a question Klíma, and Warhorse, has been thinking about. Will the force multiplier (as he describes it) of AI play a role in Warhorse's future games? For the first time in our long chat, Klíma demurs at the question. "I can't talk about it," he says. Something for us to find out, I suppose, on our next visit to Middle-earth or Bohemia.

title: I feel like I'm running a corner store in Dredd or Cyberpunk 2077
text:
Papers, Please : Your decisions as a shopkeeper have an effect. If you spot someone on the wanted list coming in to your store, you can report them to security for a reward—but keep in mind they may be members of the resistance fighting against the cruel dystopia.
Dredd : With customers coming in from the poverty-stricken lower levels and the wealthier upper levels, it feels like I'm working a shop in one of those massive towers from the Dredd movie, even though in the game's fiction I'm actually working in a cyberpunk space-station.
Strange Horticulture : My favorite shopkeeping sim is a fascinating detective game in disguise , and there's a hint of it in Probably Stolen. You can use a magnifying glass to examine items to see if they're counterfeit and as an appraisal tool to judge their value, a bit like how you search for clues to ID plants in Strange Horticulture. Fun!
Fallout : You can farm rats for their meat, set up water purification systems, scavenge through trash heaps to find scrap to turn into sellable goods... I know I'm on a space station, but it feels a little like I'm trying to earn a buck in the wasteland.
Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale : You're not just selling, you're buying, and you can haggle over prices, sometimes at the expense of your reputation. Demand in the station can change: if a mining expedition docks, for example, you can expect the prices of metals to plunge as supply explodes. You'll have to be nimble and keep your eye on what's valuable from day to day.
Cyberpunk 2077 : I probably don't need to elaborate on this one, choombatta.

title: What insiders say Halo Studios was up to before losing Halo: 'The next Halo game was years away'
text:
In the wake of Microsoft gutting Halo Studios to a skeleton crew and passing off the series to Activision, new reports from insiders tell a believable story about what was happening in Halo Studios as the plug got pulled. The accounts come from The Verge's Tom Warren (longtime Microsoft beat writer) and YouTuber Rebs Gaming (whose sources within the Halo machine are often accurate).
According to sources
The drastic cuts were a surprise to some Halo Studios employees, who had to wait hours to learn if they still had a job: "The first communication came in a public Xbox blog, before notifications were sent to employees throughout the morning." (via Warren)
The next mainline Halo game was, at minimum, "years" away (via Warren and Rebs)
No games were in full production when the layoffs happened, but work on Halo 2 and Halo 3 remakes, Halo 7, and "spinoff campaigns" was underway (via Rebs)
One of the shorter spinoff games would've been based on the First Strike novel, to be released between remakes (via Rebs)
Rebs' source also claimed that Halo Studios is now around 30 people, with Warren noting that they'll be servicing existing Halo games Infinite and Campaign Evolved. Meanwhile, Activision is building a new studio dedicated to the future of Halo.
Acknowledging that there's always more to a story than a handful of sources can cover, the picture they paint sounds very Halo Studios: slow-moving, scattered, and with one foot firmly in Halo's past. We all assumed that more remakes were in the cards, but that's looking less likely now—considering the many ways Campaign Evolved was a step back from the original, I can't decide if this is a relief of a missed opportunity.
It is sad that these people won't get a crack at Halo 7, because for all its delays and live-service fumbles , Halo Infinite grew into the best Halo since the Bungie days, and even outshined its original makers in some respects. I hope some of that talent can be aimed toward this next Halo venture.

title: World of Warcraft: Forever dev has 'no sympathy' for players kicked from the beta for offensive names: 'If you're genuinely confused, remember that it's our database, we can see every character you've created'
text:
One of the developers running the World of Warcraft: Forever beta has no patience for the people who think they can get away with naming their characters something inappropriate.
I was surprised at how many awful player names I've seen while playing the beta over the last week. WoW usually has a pretty strict filter that covers a lot of racist or disgusting names and all their permutations. But in the beta, I saw more than usual that felt like they should've been blocked at the character creation screen.
It turns out, this was a mistake on Blizzard's part, according to senior game producer Tom Ellis on X : "Our naming filter wasn’t ready to rock for dual names but we naively thought after twenty years folks knew what was and wasn’t OK and we’d be fine for a few weeks of beta till it came online."
Things were not fine from day one of the beta, which required Blizzard to manually run every name through their filter system and then double check them just in case, Ellis said.
A wave of bans went out alongside the beta's first major patch yesterday to revoke access for the worst names and force the iffy ones to be changed. This prompted some of those players to go on social media and Reddit to complain that they were wrongfully punished.
"A couple of us spent the evening reading through everything again and checked every Reddit post and Twitter and so far every one of them who's posted their three cheeky or just inappropriate names has had a 4th character they have accidentally omitted," he says.
Ellis says there isn't a new policy for WoW: Forever and that anyone with names like that "would have not been allowed in any variation of WoW at any time in its history and would have earned you a suspension."
Well honestly I should know better than to have waded into that swamp, that’s on me. Since we’re here now I’ll give one more update on this topic before getting back to actually working on launch instead of reading everyone’s hilarious variations of the N word.A couple of us… September 25, 2026
"If you're genuinely confused, remember that it's our database, we can see every character you've created, not just the one you're playing," he says. "I read the list. No sympathy. Be a better human next time."
It was very brave of Blizzard to launch what was inevitably going to be a massive beta without a working name filter. I don't envy the poor developers who have to manually go through them all as a result, but I do appreciate that there's zero tolerance for players who are abusing it. For every "Jack MeHoff" or "Ligma Bowlz" sparking delight and joy from us all, there are far nastier malefactors who should know better.
If WoW: Forever's devs want to bring back old-school social interactions in the MMO, this is the moderation approach it needs. The best moments in the beta have been the times where I've grouped up with strangers for a quick quest or saved a fellow adventurer from being mauled by several enemies at once. The last thing I want is for WoW: Forever to be ruined for anyone hoping to experience the kind of social interactions that make MMOs feel alive.

title: This 78-year-old grandmother has an insatiable lust for violence (in Fortnite)
text:
Scottish grandmother Cath Bowie's hunger for bloodshed is celebrated by thousands.
Recently named the world's oldest female Fortnite steamer by Guinness World Records, Bowie began playing the battle royale behemoth under the nom de guerre grumpygran1948 in 2017. Now streaming for an audience of over 24,000 followers, she was introduced to the game by her grandson, who—unwisely—doubted his grandmother's prospects as a conqueror.
"As a young guy he just couldn't believe that his grandma would do such a thing and suggested that nobody would join me or watch me," Bowie told Guinness World Records . "Saying that was like a red rag to a bull to me. I would show him that I could do it. 24,000+ followers later and he doesn't mention it. I wonder why?"
Given Bowie's self-professed singleminded pursuit of glorious slaughter, I can't blame her grandson for his reticence. Bowie says that during her daily Fortnite sessions, she's not playing for Victory Royales. Instead, she has a simpler, purer aim:
"The one thing I do like, you see—this is me and my challenging nature—is to go in and eliminate folk," Bowie said in a video interview with the BBC .
According to Bowie, her delight over the thunder of gunfire and the lamenting choir of her countless shattered foemen has never waned, even after nine years.
"The most important thing of all is that in all these years I have continued to enjoy every day, every week, every month and every year that I have played and streamed," she said. "I’m incredibly thankful to my wonderful family, who have encouraged me throughout the last nine years of playing, and to the many friends I’ve played with along the way."
For any others who have yearned in their later years to drink deep the red wine of battle, Bowie said you're never too old to start.
"Never let age stop you," she said, presumably flanked by heaped war-riches and the piled skulls of her slain competitors. "If I can do it, so can you."

title: The eyes of Valve's creepy portrait are glowing again
text:
The portrait of the man with red gloves is glowing again , which can only mean one thing for Deadlock players: Valve is about to drop a major new update very soon.
Real soon, in fact. The last time the portrait in the main hub started glowing was before the Old Gods, New Blood update , which introduced six new heroes, a new mode, and a bunch of other things that elevated the game from Valve's pet project to a real videogame that might actually see the light of day.
One of the developers at Valve confirmed it on Discord, too, but when we're talking about the community of players who desperately track pizza orders for signs of new updates, they'll take any extra confirmation they can get.
"Heads up we are planning on releasing the major content update early next week," the mysterious developer-ran Discord account Yoshi wrote after weeks of speculation from the community.
In typical Valve fashion, however, it hasn't said a word about what will actually be in the new update, just that it will be big. Deadlock recently overhauled its ranked mode and kicked off its first ranked season. Since then, it's just been small balance updates.
(Image credit: Tyler C. / Valve) Valve hitting the glowing eyes button sure makes it seem like there could be a new batch of heroes and revisions to the dwindling number of obviously-unfinished bits in the game. Dataminers have dug up new models for Deadlock's version of MOBA towers, which could be part of a broader visual update for the few things that still don't quite fit with its 1950s urban fantasy aesthetic. There's a rumored PvE-focused mode coming, too, but that sounds like it's a ways off if it happens at all.
You never really know what Valve has planned. For all we know, the game could have its invite-only restriction lifted and go fully into an open beta. We're probably not quite there at this point, but it's clear that a lot of work is going into polishing it into something worthy of a proper Valve game.

title: Guess who patented a new system for in-game ads
text:
Tom's Hardware and Respawn First recently reported on a fun new patent from those wiz kids at Microsoft, one that would dynamically pause your game to show you advertisements. Here are the big wham lines from the abstract of US 202610260258 A1 , "Contextually Aware Management of Interactive Software Application Access:"
"A content management system may suspend a user's interaction with the interactive software application based on the promoted content trigger event." (Emphasis mine)
"A content management system may present the promoted audiovisual content to the user."
"A content management system may establish a credit … the credit delays suspension of the user's interaction."
That's the sort of whimsical creativity that made me fall in love with games in the first place. In plain English: This is a system for showing advertisements during gameplay, one that pauses your game (suspends your interaction). Similar to ad-supported mobile games, Microsoft proposes a credit system where these tokens can be exchanged for more ad-free game time.
Microsoft explains that videogames do not lend themselves to regular commercial breaks in the same way as TV shows, necessitating a partially user-controlled, credit-based system for managing advertisement delivery. The other half of the equation: Having it monitor gameplay and avoid deploying ads during climactic or lean-forward moments. How thoughtful.
This sounds, quite frankly, god-awful. One of the worst case scenario arguments against always-online consoles and subscription-based gaming outlined in a patent. I'm not sure there is a game good enough, or an ad-supported Game Pass package cheap enough, that would make me subject myself to this. Forget the inconvenience⁠—the indignity of it all is enough to drive you to the brink.
The silver lining, if you're still rooting for Xbox⁠—it still holds some of my favorite studios hostage⁠—is that patents are not always put into practice. Seventeen years ago, Sony signaled intent to have us all stand up and shout "McDonalds" to make a vision of a burger go away, and that never happened.
The popular outrage against the patent may already be giving the planners at Microsoft pause. On the other hand: Xbox's CSO Matthew Ball is still a big believer in in-game ads . Meanwhile, The ailing titan EA has already rolled out EA Advertising , a new platform for "in-game integrations, creative partnerships, and scalable advertising capabilities." I love scalable advertising capabilities.

title: My favorite $6 RPG on Steam just got a beastmode free 'Enhanced Edition' update
text:
FlyKnight is a $6, first-person RPG in the King's Field/Lunacid mold that whips ass, looks like Old School Runescape, and feels like it could have asked for twice as much money and still been a bargain.
That alone makes it one of my easiest recommendations on Steam, but it also just got a free update of the GOTY/Enhanced/Definitive Edition variety, from its solo dev, while still only asking new players for $6 upfront⁠—$4 at the time of writing, thanks to a sale running through September 30. Here are the big Enhanced Edition additions:
Multiple difficulties, with a Miyazaki's Choice™ poison swamp exclusive to Hard
Item and enemy randomization, with savable procedural generation seeds
Four new weapon types, and an unspecified number of additions to previous weapon categories
Performance improvements "especially noticeable on Steam Deck"—which is great, because that's definitely where I most recommend playing
Graphics, UI, and balance tweaks, plus bugfixes
The update's pound-for-pound beefiness is appropriately proportional to FlyKnight's own: I loved the seven hours I spent with this game on Steam Deck last year, and always meant to revisit it⁠—now I have the perfect excuse.
FlyKnight has the vibes and the charm down, but so do a lot of entries in this growing subgenre of indie King's Field-alikes . What set it apart for me was its excellent combat. FlyKnight has this very unique, satisfying system of locational limb damage, letting you priority target weak spots or weapon-holding appendages. It also only just clicked with me how appropriate that is in a game about anthropomorphic bugs, which notably take severed limbs like champs.
It's very slow-paced, but high-skill, like a classico survival horror game. Think less dodging and i-frames, more controlling distance, taking advantage of stagger opportunities, and perfect blocking. I can't recommend FlyKnight enough at the price of "a pretty good cup of coffee," let alone "a slightly worse cup of coffee" on sale. Check it out on Steam .

title: How to open the auxiliary lines in Part 6 of Silent Hill: Townfall
text:
Key items
Code to the locker in the command centre: 0825
Key to the auxiliary room found in said locker.
A floppy disk found in the locker inside the auxiliary room.
Opening the auxiliary lines at the end of Part 6 in Silent Hill: Townfall is perhaps its most complicated yet simple puzzle. By this point in the game my brain was completely fried and my nerves were shot. So in case you're also in a bad spot, here are some tips to point you in the right direction.
Spoilers ahead for Silent Hill: Townfall
How to get to the Auxiliary Room
Before you head to the elevator and go up to the auxiliary room, you'll need to get the key. This can be found in the command centre, and the code to get into it is 0825 . Inside, you'll find the key to the auxiliary room. Now you can head downstairs to the elevator, but be warned—this is where The Weight and other monsters are lurking, so you need to be cautious. You can make a mercy dash to the elevator as the doors close quickly, but it'll be tight.
Once you've made it to the next floor, there'll be a couple of smaller monsters who you can easily circumvent. Make sure to close the door to the auxiliary room once you're inside.
How to open the auxiliary lines
(Image credit: Konami) Here you'll find a pipe running across the walls with levers at various intervals. There's also a locker and a desk with a terminal. The first step is to open the locker and find the floppy disk. Then, head to the terminal and use the floppy disk to get your clue: a bunch of lines.
Tip
(Image credit: Konami) Take a photo of the document on your phone for ease of reference.
At first glance, this could look like morse code or some other cipher, but actually it's much simpler than it seems: It shows whether each lever needs to be horizontal or vertical. But not every lever is included: only the ones which are adjacent to one white line for the first row, two lines for the second, and three lines for the third.
Auxiliary Line 1
Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Auxiliary line 1 solution : | _ | | _ | _ | |
The first line starts on the wall next to the locker, just by the white arrow at the bottom of the wall, and includes all the levers which are next to the singular white lines on the pipes. The pattern goes like this:
vertical
horizontal
vertical
vertical
horizontal
vertical
horizontal
vertical
vertical
If you've done it right the light next to the last lever should turn green.
Auxiliary Line 2
Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Auxiliary line 2 solution : | _ _ _ | _ _ | |
The second line starts on the wall next to the locker by the middle white arrow. The pattern should be:
vertical
horizontal
horizontal
horizontal
vertical
horizontal
horizontal
vertical
vertical
Again, if you've done this right, then the light next to the last lever should turn green.
Auxiliary Line 3
Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Konami Auxiliary line 3 solution : _ | | | _ | _ |
The third line starts on the opposite wall to the other two, above the second light that just turned green and the pattern should be:
horizontal
vertical
vertical
vertical
horizontal
vertical
horizontal
vertical
Again, if you've done it right the final light will turn green. That's the end of that, and now you can leave the room (be careful of the creepies), head back to the elevator, and make your way back to the control room (avoiding The Weight and other monsters) to wrap up your segment in the command centre.

title: I did the math on my Wardogs XP grind, and now I wish I hadn't
text:
I've had this goal in the back of my head to unlock all the Medic gear in Wardogs so I can become the best sawbones on the server. There's only one piece I still don't have—a medical bag that can both revive and heal teammates in one item. It's unlocked at Medic level 24, which doesn't sound so bad, since I've already reached level 18 over my first 30 hours of Wardogs.
But this week I noticed my steady Medic rise had slowed considerably. I had been ranking up every one or two rounds, but now I'm lucky to climb a rank over a whole night of play. I'm doing just as well in matches—better than ever, actually, with the addition of defibrillators and stronger medkits—so that's not the issue.
For the first time, I made note of the XP thresholds for leveling up and compared where I'm at to my goal. I wish I hadn't. So far I've gained 17 levels with 177,619 Medic XP. Level 24, just seven ranks later, will require 337,000 XP. So while it looks like I'm gaining on that useful medicine bag, I'm actually just 52% of the way there .
So this is the brutal Wardogs grind I've been hearing about. Bummer.
The mountain
I was curious how that last 48% will translate to playtime and matches—maybe it'll go by faster than it sounds—so I did an unscientific test: I played an average match with my typical focus on revives and healing. For the record: I'm an OK player at best. To maximise XP gains, I also brought an SMG and purchased stims to administer to teammates.
Over a 50-minute match on the winning team, this was my scoreline:
Medic XP earned
Cash earned
Revives
Kills
Assists
9,995
$62,215
15 (2nd highest)
2
5
A pretty low kill game, admittedly. Our team repeatedly pulled the zone to our walled-off FOB, so there was a lot of time spent dragging bodies away from mortar barrages. If I keep playing like this, I'd unlock the medicine bag in 16 more matches, or ~13 hours of playtime .
I reckon that, depending on who you are, that either sounds surprisingly reasonable or totally deflating. It's disheartening for me, because these days I only play games for two or three hours on the nights that I play anything at all. By my standards, I've been going hard on Wardogs these past two weeks and yet I'm still at least a week away from unlocking this singular item.
Is this mountainous XP climb exactly what Bulkhead had in mind, and if so, is it good? It's a question the Wardogs community is grappling with every day , and opinions are all over the map. Some think the XP milestones increase too quickly, others think the grind would be fine if not for the planned seasonal wipes, and some firmly believe that Wardogs needs its massive XP grind to stay interesting.
(Image credit: Team17) It's an issue of degrees. To what degree is Wardogs meant to accommodate players with limited time, and how much should Bulkhead cater to the diehards racking up hundreds of hours? Complex multiplayer games have a way of splintering into differing perceived states depending on the beholder's skill and commitment level.
Changing the state of XP and cash is both a philosophical and balancing consideration: If it takes less XP to get my precious medicine bag or RPG or attack helicopter, that also affects how quickly powerful items become prominent in matches throughout a season, and Wardogs' meta progression flattens. But if nothing changes, then a player at my level may never unlock some items before the next wipe—fair, but not fun in the long term.
Bulkhead is taking in all the feedback around grind, and has alluded to future features that will shake up the grind from season-to-season, but hasn't commented on specific changes yet. Its first major patch since early access launch is still a few weeks away—season 2 begins October 15, and will wipe everyone back to level 1. Back to the base of the mountain.

title: A running tally of the most ridiculous things AI bigwigs have said so far
text:
If there's anything the leaders of the AI era love more than watching the billion-dollar valuations of their companies tick up, it's warning us that the software making them rich might just destroy the world.
AI is going to kill us all. Now, can we have more money for data centers, please?
Their next favorite activity? Coming up with trendy phrases that either explain how toooootally smart the next upcoming AI model will be or justify why their previous claims of imminent AI sentience haven't quite arrived on schedule.
These buzzwords and prognostications are hard to keep track of and even harder to parse. With new whoppers arriving every week, we're spinning up a running log that we can reference whenever we need to recall how often AI thought leaders contradict themselves and each other, and how constantly they move the goal posts.
We'll update this blog whenever we notice a particularly absurd, empty, or unbelievable remark from an industry whose astronomical valuation is entirely down to the dubious claim that large language models are both going to destroy and save humanity. We're starting with just the last couple months of gobsmacking quotes, because going much further back would be too miserable.
But first, it might be helpful to set the stage:
8 times AI guys declared AGI was right around the corner:
AGI, or "artificial general intelligence," is often cited as a goal for AI development and spoken of with near-mythical reverence. Here's how OpenAI describes it:
"If AGI is successfully created, this technology could help us elevate humanity by increasing abundance, turbocharging the global economy, and aiding in the discovery of new scientific knowledge that changes the limits of possibility.
"AGI has the potential to give everyone incredible new capabilities; we can imagine a world where all of us have access to help with almost any cognitive task, providing a great force multiplier for human ingenuity and creativity.
"On the other hand, AGI would also come with serious risk of misuse, drastic accidents, and societal disruption. Because the upside of AGI is so great, we do not believe it is possible or desirable for society to stop its development forever; instead, society and the developers of AGI have to figure out how to get it right."

December 2025 : "Musk said that xAI could achieve artificial general intelligence, which matches or exceeds human intelligence, in the next few years, even as soon as 2026"

November 2024 : Altman says AGI is coming in 2025
April 2024 : Elon Musk says "If you define AGI (artificial general intelligence) as smarter than the smartest human, I think it's probably next year, within two years"

title: Drop everything and grab the popcorn: Majuular's 4.5-hour documentary on Ultima Online is here to devour your weekend
text:
I'll make this quick: Whatever you had planned for the weekend, you've got to carve four-and-a-half hours out for a last-minute swerve into the late '90s. Six months in the making, YouTube essayist Majuular is back with the (I believe) penultimate video in his multi-year Ultima series. "This one was a doozy," he wrote in the comments. It's Ultima Online.
"From its unlikely formation at the behest of Richard Garriott and Starr Long, to its tempering at the hands of Raph Koster and his team of Multi-User Dungeon enthusiasts, to its changing identity in the face of competition, to its incalculable influence, this is the story of Ultima Online," the description reads. If you get the Ultima Online bug after watching the documentary, good news: it's still very much playable on both official servers and fan ones. Majuular highlighted the server he played on, In Mani Ylem , which aims to recapture the late '90s experience.
You can find the entire video series in a playlist here , and I can't recommend watching them highly enough. In late 2025 we published a feature story about Majuular's quest to chronicle the making of Richard Garriott's genre-defining series, and how that mission unexpectedly catapulted him to YouTube success with more than 200,000 followers. It's a good read—and won't take you quite as long as watching all the videos.
'A good idea, infinite drive, and lots of Diet Pepsi': How YouTube essayist Majuular's life changed course telling the story of Ultima across 2 years and more than 20 hours of documentaries
The Majuular Ultima Retrospective embodies the fastidious, affectionate critique that is gaming YouTube at its best. Many are multi-hour features that trace Ultima's burgeoning influence on both western and Japanese roleplaying games, discuss the human stories and context around its creation, and actually involve the dirty work of playing the games while analyzing Ultima's lore on its own terms.

title: Former Starfield designer says Bethesda's sci-fi RPG probably won't get a sequel, because the original wasn't 'anywhere near successful enough'
text:
I wasn't expecting to see a Starfield sequel any time soon, given it took Bethesda eight years to make its sci-fi RPG and the studio is currently focussed on The Elder Scrolls 6 . But if the words of Starfield's former systems designer are anything to go by, we may not see a sequel to Bethesda's first new IP in 25 years at all.
In an interview with FRVR (via VGC ), Bethesda veteran Kurt Kuhlmann explained why he doubts the studio will ever return to Starfield: "I would be very surprised", said Kuhlmann, who left Bethesda after Starfield was released. "I don't think Starfield was anywhere near successful enough to do a Starfield 2."
While specific sales figures for Starfield haven't been released, Bethesda's sci-fi RPG is estimated to have generated $300 million in revenue as of April this year. This would make Starfield profitable based on its reported budget of $200 million , but it still has a long way to go before it reaches Skyrim levels of success . Since Xbox has reportedly expressed a desire to focus on its major franchises , it seems likely that Bethesda will prioritise The Elder Scrolls and Fallout over Starfield.
Nonetheless, Kuhlmann thinks this may represent a missed opportunity for Bethesda to build on the lessons learned creating Starfield and create something truly special: "It's in a way, too bad, because I think with the lessons learned on Starfield, a Starfield 2 could have been much closer to the game that Todd had [in mind]."
One issue Kuhlmann thinks a sequel could address is Starfield's outpost building mechanic, which Kuhlmann believes was added to Starfield somewhat arbitrarily and wasn't sufficiently baked into the core experience. "You can build a base anywhere you want on a planet. For what it is, as a standalone system, it's cool, but it's not nearly as integrated with the rest of the game," he said.
In addition, Kuhlmann pointed out that Bethesda faced a similar problem with Fallout 4 , and failed to learn the lesson. "It caused problems for it to be integrated with the story and the missions and stuff in Fallout 4, so it was kind of put to the side. Which begs the question of, well, why is it still in the game?" But apparently the decision to keep the system in Starfield was "above" him. "You might say 'Well, we shouldn't have it then if we're not going to integrate it with the story, then it's just this system sitting over there with a massive amount of work involved."
Personally, I think Starfield's problems were less to do with a superfluous outpost building mechanic, and more to do with narrative and systems design that was outclassed by games like Baldur's Gate 3 and even felt dated compared to older RPGs like The Witcher 3 . Yet while a full sequel for Starfield may be unlikely, Bethesda has demonstrated long-term commitment to the original game thus far. It has continued to support the base game with both free updates and DLC , while in July, the studio stated that Starfield remains "an important part of our future".

title: It took CD Projekt two years to design Phantom Liberty's Chimera Tank boss fight: 'We were iterating over and over'
text:
One of the most striking early sequences in Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty is its Chimera Tank boss fight, in which V and President Myers battle an enormous, Ghost in the Shell-inspired spider-tank in the bowels of a Barghest facility. The battle forms the explosive culmination of Phantom Liberty's opening act, and CD Projekt recently revealed just what it took to get the sequence where they wanted it.
Speaking on CD Projekt's official AnsweRED podcast (via Eurogamer ), Phantom Liberty's game director Gabe Amatangelo, and creative director Igor Sarzyński discussed various production challenges the studio faced during Cyberpunk 2077 's creation, bringing up the Chimera Tank as an example. "Sometimes we're making content that's a nexus point of different disciplines, the Chimera is a great example of that," Amatangelo said. "It was gameplay, narrative, art, worldbuilding."
Amatangelo explained that CD Projekt wanted the Chimera Tank to "terrify" players with its weapons, and that there were "so many moving parts" to balance appropriately for the sequence to work. "Sometimes it was too gameplay [focussed], sometimes it was too narrative, sometimes too art direction. It was about striking a balance and I think the three of us got into it and went: 'Okay, beat-by-beat, let's do this.'"
According to Paweł Mielniczuk, Phantom Liberty's art director and the podcast's co-host, creating the boss fight was a years-long process. "I think when we were iterating, it was two years to make this boss fight work," he explained. Later in the chat, Mielniczuk stated the tank went through "four" different iterations that involved "changing equipment [and] the weapons", while Sarzyński claimed that the Chimera's construction represents "one of the most expensive art assets I think ever."
It's interesting to hear CD Projekt discuss the encounter's development, especially since, when I played it around Phantom Liberty's launch, I thought it would have benefited from slightly more balancing. Slowly blasting it to bits was one of the more gruelling parts of Phantom Liberty, and reminded me a lot of the unexpectedly punishing battle with The Toad Prince in The Witcher 3: Hearts of Stone .
Nonetheless, fighting the Chimera Tank is certainly memorable, while Phantom Liberty more broadly is one of the best things I've played this decade. I'm keen to see how CDP takes all the lessons it's learned making Cyberpunk into the sequel, though we've got several years, a Witcher 3 expansion , and The Witcher 4 to come before we see it.
